headline: Three-Way Rig, One Eel, 38 Inches — Plum Gut Delivers on the Neap
subhead: The first-quarter neap is softening the rip and opening a wider window for eels and swimbaits, while fluke keep grinding steady across the zone.
body_markdown:
Three-way rig, twelve-inch eel, second hour of the outgoing at Plum Gut — I felt the take stop me cold before the current even had it, and thirty-eight inches of bass came up through the froth like it owned the rip. That's the fish that told me the neap was already changing things out here, days ahead of schedule.

We hit the first-quarter neap today, and anybody who's fished the Gut long enough knows what that means: the 5-knot freight train that usually runs through there on a big tide backs off, and instead of one violent ten-minute window at the peak of the ebb, you get a longer stretch where you can actually work an eel or a swimbait through the structure without getting swept sideways into the rocks. I fished the last two tide changes with a shad-style swimbait — a six-inch paddle tail on a three-way rig, sixty-pound fluoro leader, three ounces of dropper weight — dragged along the break where the reef drops into the channel on the east side of the Gut, worked slow on the bottom the way you'd work a jig for cod. Two fish over thirty inches in two evenings, both right on the tide change, both eating the bait as it swung off the edge and stalled in the eddy behind the rock pile.

The fluke bite has been the most dependable thing in this whole zone for weeks and it hasn't slowed down. Plum Gut structure is holding keepers mixed in with plenty of short fish — enough shorts that you grind through some throwbacks to find dinner, but the keepers are there. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, drifted slow with the current over the rock piles in twenty-five to thirty-five feet, have been the ticket. Had a client stick a sea bass in there too — 28 inches, better than five pounds, came off the same structure on a chartreuse bucktail meant for fluke. Not a fish you plan for in the Gut, but it tells you that rip is holding more than just bass and fluke right now.

Water's sitting around 69 to 70 degrees from New London out toward Montauk, which is comfortable for everything we're chasing — not so warm that the bass have gone strictly nocturnal like they have west of here, but warm enough that low-light windows are still your best bet for size. Dawn and dusk at the Race have been better than midday, plain and simple. I worked the west end of the Race at first light three mornings this week, throwing a Super Strike darter and a 2-ounce bucktail with a white shad tail through the eddies that stack along the north edge of the current, and picked up bass mid-twenties to low-thirties on the darter worked slow through the slack pockets where the rip folds back on itself. Nothing over 34 inches, but steady enough I wasn't standing there wondering if I'd made a mistake.

Bluefish are showing up along the same current edges, and when they show, they don't mess around. I've watched boils break right on the surface where the rip meets slack water off Fishers Island Sound — cast a metal into that seam, a Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster, and you're hooked up before the lure sinks a foot. These aren't cocktail blues either — some of these are jumbos, four and five pounds, slashing bait right on top. We flagged this pattern last week — called the Race and Plum Gut for sight-casting to breaking fish, and the blues are giving us exactly that right now, even if the albies haven't shown yet. If you see the boil, don't long-bomb it. Feather the cast right into the seam where the current's breaking and let it sink a second before you start the retrieve.

Porgies are still stacked on the rock piles around Orient Point and off Fishers Island in fifteen to twenty-five feet — nothing exciting to write home about, but if you want a bent rod and a bucket of dinner, a hi-lo rig with squid strips on that structure will keep you busy between tide changes. Weakfish have been scattered at best — I've heard of a few coming out of the deeper holes off Orient on bucktails tipped with squid, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

Here's what I'd do this week: fish the neap while it lasts. The softer current in the Gut and the Race should hold for several more days before the tides build back toward the next moon, and that gives you a wider window to work an eel or a swimbait through the heaviest structure without it getting ripped out of the strike zone in ten seconds flat. I'd be on the water for the tide change at Plum Gut at first light or last light, working the eastern edge where the reef drops off, and I'd have a bucktail rigged and ready in case the fluke show up under the same structure — because right now, that's a real possibility on every single drift.

If the wind stays out of the south like it has been, expect the surface to stay clean enough to sight-fish those bluefish boils off Fishers Island Sound through the week. And keep an eye on the water temps ticking up — once the low seventies show up consistently out here, the false albies and bonito that have been working their way east through the Sound all summer are going to start showing on the same rips we're fishing bass and blues on right now. Not there yet. But I'm carrying a bag of small metals in the boat just in case.
